newsitem.title: CHINA: China bars deposed leader from statesman's funeral.
newsitem.headline: China bars deposed leader from statesman's funeral.

text.p: China's former Communist Party chief Zhao Ziyang, purged after the army crushed demonstrations for democracy in 1989, has been barred from attending the funeral of elder statesman Peng Zhen, a source said on Monday.

Diplomats say China's current leadership remains nervous about the lingering influence and ambitions of Zhao, 78, whose liberal political and economic policies made him popular in the party and among the public.

Zhao had asked for permission to attend the funeral of Peng in Beijing on Monday, but his successor, Jiang Zemin, vetoed the plan, said the source close to Zhao, who asked not to be identified. No reason was given.
The People's Daily, mouthpiece of the Communist Party, paid tribute to Peng on Monday, giving a half-page spread to photographs of the party veteran, who died in Beijing on April 26 at the age of 95.
The funeral is expected to receive widespread publicity on the nightly evening television news and in official newspapers.
The leadership fears Zhao could be a wild card if he were to re-emerge from the political wilderness in a post-Deng Xiaoping power struggle, diplomats say.
Zhao returned to Beijing on May 2 after travelling outside the Chinese capital for 4-1/2 months, said the source.
Zhao was in the eastern city of Hangzhou when Deng, China's paramount leader, died on February 19 and he was barred by Jiang from attending Deng's funeral in Beijing on February 25.
Zhao left Hangzhou for his old political power base, southwestern Sichuan province, in March before returning to the capital last week, the source said.
Deng had named Zhao as his successor in 1987 only to sack him two years later for sympathising with student demonstrators.
Zhao has not been seen in public since May 19, 1989 when he visited students in Beijing's Tiananmen Square and tearfully called on them to end their demonstrations.
On June 3 and 4, troops backed by tanks stormed the city centre, crushing the demonstrations with heavy loss of life.
Zhao was accused by his enemies of backing the "counter-revolutionary turmoil" and of trying to split the party.
He has lived under virtual house arrest until recently at his home in Beijing and requires permission from the leadership to travel.
